I am starting this journal to log my journey to hopefully becoming a great trader. I've spent quite a while reading DrSwing's journal and what an inspiration and learning experience it was. Feel free to be as hard and critical as possible on me during my endeavor. I must succeed, I will succeed. Thank you all in advance. Price action zone, it does what it says on the tin. look for our zones the contain price between to distinct levels. These levels are where decisions on value are made, they are not exact, I use my paz's a a guide an then look for the FL's and FTR's that are relevant. You can see the one example I have put on the chart where we have engulfed in to a new paz, but more importantly we have engulfed the important demand. We then engulf the decision to leave the previous zone. We have CP'd away from the edge of the lower zone so the demand is the last set of orders at the edge of the cp, we target the furthest set of orders in the zone above. Whenever you have a fresh FL near an FTR, we should always expect price to FO to the fresh FL. When thinking in like an IT, we want to get in at the best possible price. In the chart below, we see we our FTR formed, after the engulf. We can see above the FTR there was a fresh FL. Price FO'd our FTR and entered the fresh FL above before breaking down. This is seem time and time again in the charts. Whenever there is a FRESH FL in close proximity of an FTR always expect price to FO. When placing a TP, I normally TP at the next opposite FTR/FL. I marked up a quick chart showing the way I read price. In the chart below you can see in the initial down move, several bullish FTRs were engulfed. Once price decided to turn around without reaching it's target, we would have entered a sell at the origin, and our TP would have been the FTR that price was initially attracted to but never reached. Remember, the space between FTRs are a type of PAZ. So when price enters a PAZ it's going to go to the opposing side. It would be very difficult to take a trade based on the information provided on your chart. We have to look further left to know what the low marked in the chart below is a reaction to. That low could very well have been the end of a retrace that hadn't yet hit a target, it could be a break into a PAZ, and it is also possible that it is an engulf of an entire zone. When I began RTM, I thought I could pick any random low or high, and a break of that level automatically means the FTR following that break was important. It is always important to look "left and then left again" to know what that low or high is a reaction to. Remember we are reading the entire market. (FTB). So look to see where price failed to get back into a flag and you can guess there are still sell orders there. Does this make any sense at all? To answer your question and frustration about which LS to use and which one is important, I do have a better understanding now than before when I first took the https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2033-josh1125-rtm-journey?start=475 8/32 7/27/2018 Josh1125 RTM Journey - Page 20 - RTM Community course. I was frustrated like you, wondering which one will bounce price and which one HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT won't. Here is what I found. We look for LS of a FL that broke another FL to the left, just like a QM. For example, your trend is up and now you form a LS. That LS needs to break a UFL to the left for it to become important. Once we have that, then we marke the high and low of that FL and look for the kink on the right side for PA when price returns to it. Now, we don't know if the kink (on the right side) will hold price or if price will break thru...... hence that is the reason we want to see the the ENG (then the QM/DM) before taking the trade. I find higher time frame LS especially on the Day/Week/Month to be stronger than the lower time frame. The other thing that we must look for in the kink is that have price come up to take the orders in the kink. If it did, then that kink is less likely to hold price. If there are clean orders in the quick, then you are likely to get a bounce. Hopes this helps. . After reading markepedia and the articles several times and several journals, I still struggled with how to it all fits together. Individually, I could identify everything, but putting the puzzle pieces together was difficult. Well today I had what I think was my biggest ahah moment. Something finally clicked after reading once again one of IF's article on Past, Approach and Reaction. 1. Price first has to create a zone. We use FL (RBR and DBD) , FTR, S/D(RBD, DBR), and S/R -. These zones happen in the past, and we want to identify those zones as areas of interest. 2. As price approaches the zone, we pay attention to whether or not price shows compression or if it gives a the 3 Drive pattern. -. This is important, because price this gives us clues on whether or not that zone will hold. 3. The Reaction. This is where we watch the PA in or around the already established zone. In order to achieve our maximum R:R we would switch to a LTF to watch the PA play out. This is where we look for Engulf, QM, Diamond, and Can Can. - This comes AFTER our HTF zone has been established and price has come back. Please feel free to correct me wherever you see error in my thinking. We have CP'd away from the edge of the lower zone so the demand is the last set of orders at the edge of the cp, we target the furthest set of orders in the zone above. Whenever you have a fresh FL near an FTR, we should always expect price to FO to the fresh FL. When thinking in like an IT, we want to get in at the best possible price. In the chart below, we see we our FTR formed, after the engulf. We can see above the FTR there was a fresh FL. Price FO'd our FTR and entered the fresh FL above before breaking down. This is seem time and time again in the charts. Whenever there is a FRESH FL in close proximity of an FTR always expect price to FO. When placing a TP, I normally TP at the next opposite FTR/FL. I marked up a quick chart showing the way I read price. In the chart below you can see in the initial down move, several bullish FTRs were engulfed. Once price decided to turn around without reaching it's target, we would have entered a sell at the origin, and our TP would have been the FTR that price was initially attracted to but never reached. Remember, the space between FTRs are a type of PAZ. So when price enters a PAZ it's going to go to the opposing side. Hope this helps a little. victoryong wrote: Hey Josh1125, Would like to pick your mind on few subject, how do you decide on the origin of move and how do you decide where to place your TP? It would be very difficult to take a trade based on the information provided on your chart. We have to look further left to know what the low marked in the chart below is a reaction to. That low could very well have been the end of a retrace that hadn't yet hit a target, it could be a break into a PAZ, and it is also possible that it is an engulf of an entire zone. When I began RTM, I thought I could pick any random low or high, and a break of that level automatically means the FTR following that break was important. It is always important to look "left and then left again" to know what that low or high is a reaction to. Remember we are reading the entire market. We often think that price should reverse at given level and we are fixated on this one scenario. This can be bad because: - if price does something else we are suprised and strong emotion are more likely to occur - it is harder to choose correct trade management So, for example I'm watching MPL of this FL on ucad. And I see 4 likely scenarios. One of them is of course stop out and loss. To answer your question and frustration about which LS to use and which one is important, I do have a better understanding now than before when I first took the https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2033-josh1125-rtm-journey?start=475 8/32 7/27/2018 Josh1125 RTM Journey - Page 20 - RTM Community course. I was frustrated like you, wondering which one will bounce price and which one HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT won't. Here is what I found. We look for LS of a FL that broke another FL to the left, just like a QM. For example, your trend is up and now you form a LS. That LS needs to break a UFL to the left for it to become important. Once we have that, then we marke the high and low of that FL and look for the kink on the right side for PA when price returns to it. Now, we don't know if the kink (on the right side) will hold price or if price will break thru...... hence that is the reason we want to see the the ENG (then the QM/DM) before taking the trade. I find higher time frame LS especially on the Day/Week/Month to be stronger than the lower time frame. The other thing that we must look for in the kink is that have price come up to take the orders in the kink. If it did, then that kink is less likely to hold price. If there are clean orders in the quick, then you are likely to get a bounce. Hopes this helps. . Individually, I could identify everything, but putting the puzzle pieces together was difficult. Well today I had what I think was my biggest ahah moment. Something finally clicked after reading once again one of IF's article on Past, Approach and Reaction. 1. Price first has to create a zone. We use FL (RBR and DBD) , FTR, S/D(RBD, DBR), and S/R -. These zones happen in the past, and we want to identify those zones as areas of interest. 2. As price approaches the zone, we pay attention to whether or not price shows compression or if it gives a the 3 Drive pattern. -. This is important, because price this gives us clues on whether or not that zone will hold. 3. The Reaction. This is where we watch the PA in or around the already established zone. In order to achieve our maximum R:R we would switch to a LTF to watch the PA play out. This is where we look for Engulf, QM, Diamond, and Can Can. - This comes AFTER our HTF zone has been established and price has come back. Please feel free to correct me wherever you see error in my thinking. Base, flag, pole. The base and the flag are two different zones. The space between the base and flag which is the pole is what I use for my PAZ. Once price engulfs either the flag or the base, price then is free to move to the opposite side. There aren't really any orders inside the pole. So when price starts in one direction, it won't stop until it runs into more orders. milkeyway wrote: Hi Josh. How do you use PAZ ? Price action zone, it does what it says on the tin. look for our zones the contain price between to distinct levels. These levels are where decisions on value are made, they are not exact, I use my paz's a a guide an then look for the FL's and FTR's that are relevant. You can see the one example I have put on the chart where we have engulfed in to a new paz, but more importantly we have engulfed the important demand. We then engulf the decision to leave the previous zone. We have CP'd away from the edge of the lower zone so the demand is the last set of orders at the edge of the cp, we target the furthest set of orders in the zone above. Whenever you have a fresh FL near an FTR, we should always expect price to FO to the fresh FL. When thinking in like an IT, we want to get in at the best possible price. When placing a TP, I normally TP at the next opposite FTR/FL. I marked up a quick chart showing the way I read price. In the chart below you can see in the initial down move, several bullish FTRs were engulfed. Once price decided to turn around without reaching it's target, we would have entered a sell at the origin, and our TP would have been the FTR that price was initially attracted to but never reached. Remember, the space between FTRs are a type of PAZ. So when price enters a PAZ it's going to go to the opposing side. It would be very difficult to take a trade based on the information provided on your chart. We have to look further left to know what the low marked in the chart below is a reaction to. That low could very well have been the end of a retrace that hadn't yet hit a target, it could be a break into a PAZ, and it is also possible that it is an engulf of an entire zone. When I began RTM, I thought I could pick any random low or high, and a break of that level automatically means the FTR following that break was important. It is always important to look "left and then left again" to know what that low or high is a reaction to. Remember we are reading the entire market. My favorite trades are those that return to a flag after it's been established. So first you can look left to see what the high of the flag is reacting to. Then you can wait for the flag to be fully formed. Then wait for price to leave the flag and then return to it, or not as the case may be (FTR). Even returning to it a second time is often very good. (FTB). So look to see where price failed to get back into a flag and you can guess there are still sell orders there. Does this make any sense at all? I was frustrated like you, wondering which one will bounce price and which one HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT won't. Here is what I found. We look for LS of a FL that broke another FL to the left, just like a QM. For example, your trend is up and now you form a LS. That LS needs to break a UFL to the left for it to become important. Once we have that, then we marke the high and low of that FL and look for the kink on the right side for PA when price returns to it. Now, we don't know if the kink (on the right side) will hold price or if price will break thru...... hence that is the reason we want to see the the ENG (then the QM/DM) before taking the trade. I find higher time frame LS especially on the Day/Week/Month to be stronger than the lower time frame. The other thing that we must look for in the kink is that have price come up to take the orders in the kink. If it did, then that kink is less likely to hold price. If there are clean orders in the quick, then you are likely to get a bounce. Hopes this helps. . After reading markepedia and the articles several times and several journals, I still struggled with how to it all fits together. Individually, I could identify everything, but putting the puzzle pieces together was difficult. Well today I had what I think was my biggest ahah moment. Something finally clicked after reading once again one of IF's article on Past, Approach and Reaction. 1. Price first has to create a zone. We use FL (RBR and DBD) , FTR, S/D(RBD, DBR), and S/R -. These zones happen in the past, and we want to identify those zones as areas of interest. 2. As price approaches the zone, we pay attention to whether or not price shows compression or if it gives a the 3 Drive pattern. -. This is important, because price this gives us clues on whether or not that zone will hold. 3. The Reaction. This is where we watch the PA in or around the already established zone. In order to achieve our maximum R:R we would switch to a LTF to watch the PA play out. This is where we look for Engulf, QM, Diamond, and Can Can. - This comes AFTER our HTF zone has been established and price has come back. Please feel free to correct me wherever you see error in my thinking. Base, flag, pole. The base and the flag are two different zones. The space between the base and flag which is the pole is what I use for my PAZ. Once price engulfs either the flag or the base, price then is free to move to the opposite side. There aren't really any orders inside the pole. So when price starts in one direction, it won't stop until it runs into more orders. milkeyway wrote: Hi Josh. How do you use PAZ ?
